Wednesday, September 2 TODAY TOMORROW WEEKEND MONTH

6:30 PM
UNIONDOCS PRESENTS: WELFARE
by Frederick Wiseman
1975, 167 min, 16mm-to-DCP
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

Film Notes

Frederick Wiseman’s WELFARE (1975) depicts the nature and complexity of the welfare system in sequences illustrating the staggering diversity of problems that constitute welfare: housing, unemployment, divorce, medical and psychiatric problems, abandoned and abused children, and the elderly. These issues are presented in a context where welfare workers as well as clients struggle to cope with and interpret the laws and regulations that govern their work and life.

We’re excited to be partnering with UnionDocs for this screening, which represents the opening night of their two-week intensive workshop, “Wiseman’s New York”. Produced by UnionDocs and hosted by Genevieve Yue, this program is an in-depth exploration of Wiseman’s relationship to his most revisited location: New York City. Across 10 days, Yue will guide participants through a survey of Wiseman’s New York films, alongside visits to the institutions, neighborhoods, and civic spaces they document. Throughout the program, Yue is joined by filmmakers, critics, artists, and community members whose work is in conversation with Wiseman’s films, from a range of perspectives. Through screenings, discussions, site visits, and conversations, participants will consider how Wiseman’s extraordinary attention to place, labor, and public life continues to shape documentary practice today.

Joining Genevieve Yue for the introduction to WELFARE will be musician, composer, writer, and Saturday Night Live musical director Lenny Pickett, who worked with Wiseman on an operatic adaptation of WELFARE (among other projects).

For more info about UnionDocs’ workshop, “Wiseman’s New York”, visit: https://uniondocs.org/wisemans-new-york/

Thursday, September 3

7:30 PM
MIX NYC PRESENTS: EARLY INTERIORITY: VINTAGE TRANS CINEMA
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

Film Notes

This program gathers rare vintage short films that open a portal to trans feminine interior life between 1967 and 1982. We meet these women in moments of quiet confidence, everyday mundanity, and enduring glamour. Through deeply intimate portraits, these films unearth buried pieces of trans history while illuminating how the world has long constricted trans women’s freedom to be. Made under a police state, these portraits mirror the experiences of trans femmes today. Each woman captured becomes a living testament to ancestral resilience and the enduring necessity of trans documentation.

This program is co-curated by Thee Rose and Rosalina Michele for MIX NYC, one of the oldest queer experimental film festivals in the world.

Special thanks to the Institute for Studies on Latin American Art (ISLAA); to Bradford Nordeen for providing the digital exhibition files; and to the Film-Makers' Coop for providing the 16mm prints.

Nikolai Ursin BEHIND EVERY GOOD MAN (1967, 8 min, 16mm)
Marguerite Paris ALL WOMEN ARE EQUAL (1972, 15 min, 16mm. Preserved by MIX NYC and the Women’s Film Preservation Fund via New York Women in Film & Television.)
Joseph Horning VALERIE (1975, 16 min, 16mm-to-DCP)
Manuel Herreros de Lemos & Mateo Manaure Arilla TRANS (1982, 22 min, 16mm-to-DCP)

Total running time: ca. 65 min.

Followed by a discussion between curators Thee Rose and Rosalina Michele, moderated by Kristen Lovell (co-director of THE STROLL).

Friday, September 4

6:45 PM
WHAT GODMILOW TAUGHT
by Mireia Sallarès
In English and Catalan with English subtitles, 2010-14, 46 min, digital
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: WHAT GODMILOW TAUGHT

Film Notes

FILMMAKER IN PERSON!

In 2012, Jill Godmilow wrote to Mireia Sallarès, moved by the film she had made in Mexico about women’s orgasms. For Godmilow, who offered to help distribute the film in the U.S., LAS MUERTES CHIQUITAS (THE LITTLE DEATHS) is not a documentary about a problem of Mexican women, it is a film about orgasms as a political issue that affects everyone and raises the question of who can take responsibility for it by speaking out. How to take responsibility for our problems, how to take charge of them by making political films, was the concern that had led Godmilow to engage years earlier with Harun Farocki’s documentary INEXTINGUISHABLE FIRE, which showed how napalm production during the Vietnam War effectively exempted its makers from any responsibility for it. The fact that Farocki’s film had not been seen in the U.S. and that the problem it raised had not gone away, Godmilow decided to recreate it, in order to involve herself in the problem and put it back into circulation. As a statement about what it means today to be an author, and taking account of this complexity by broadening and politicizing the chain of authorship, she titled her replica WHAT FAROCKI TAUGHT. The present film, WHAT GODMILOW TAUGHT (2014), is a film conversation in which Mireia Sallarès captures Jill Godmilow’s commitment to a political life. Sallarès’s film engages with an artistic practice in which having an idea entails a responsibility, and in which grappling with a political problem requires collaborating with others to make useful films.

Followed by:
Jill Godmilow ECSTATIC ORGASM 7.5-min excerpt from an unfinished film, digital

Total running time: ca. 60 min.

8:45 PM
WHAT FAROCKI TAUGHT + SCUM MANIFESTO
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: WHAT GODMILOW TAUGHT

Film Notes

Jill Godmilow
WHAT FAROCKI TAUGHT
1997, 30 min, 16mm. Made in collaboration with Gloria Jean Masciarotte & Ted Mandell.
WHAT FAROCKI TAUGHT is literally and stubbornly a remake – that is, a perfect replica in color and in English, of Harun Farocki’s black-and-white, 1969 German language film, INEXTINGUISHABLE FIRE. Taking as its subject the political and formal strategies of Farocki’s film about the development of Napalm B by Dow Chemical during the Vietnam War, Godmilow’s unabashedly perfect copy reopens Walter Benjamin’s discussion of art in the age of mechanical reproduction. WHAT FAROCKI TAUGHT thus becomes an agit-prop challenge to the cinéma vérité documentary’s representation of information, history, politics, and “real” human experience. Because Farocki’s film was not in distribution in the U.S. at the time, WHAT FAROCKI TAUGHT was conceived as a gesture of film distribution – taking this small, film footnote to a war, a barnacle stuck on the side of the moth-balled vessel of Vietnam, flicking it forward past the recent, more sophisticated, and successful technologies of Panama and the Persian Gulf, to see if the “ping” of recognition and the radical potential of the documentary film project could be revived.

Jill Godmilow
SCUM MANIFESTO
2016, 27 min, digital. Made in collaboration with Joanna Krakowska & Magda Mosiewicz.
When Sherry Millner and Ernest Larsen, the producers of the Facets DVD compilation “Disruptive Film”, couldn’t clear the rights to Delphine Seyrig and Carole Roussopoulos’s 1976 French film, SCUM MANIFESTO, they contacted Jill Godmilow, Queen of Replicas (see WHAT FAROCKI TAUGHT), who decided to produce a perfect Polish copy of this landmark film about the 1967 feminist manifesto – this time with Polish performers and current Polish newsreel of goings-on in the newly super-nationalist Polish state. Exactly as in the 1976 French film, the Poles translate then type up, phrase-by-phrase, Valerie Solanas’s still outrageous and profoundly useful 1967 text, which begins, “Life in this society being, at best, an utter bore and no aspect of society being at all relevant to women, there remains to civic-minded, responsible, thrill-seeking females only to overthrow the government, eliminate the money system, institute complete automation and destroy the male sex.”

Total running time: ca. 60 min.

8:00 PM
ROY COHN/JACK SMITH
by Jill Godmilow
1995, 88 min, 16mm
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: WHAT GODMILOW TAUGHT

Film Notes

From one of the seminal theatrical events of the 1990s – Ron Vawter’s extraordinary performance piece ROY COHN/JACK SMITH – Godmilow crafts a dramatically deft, comic, and terrifying film diptych. Roy Cohn, the homophobic right-wing lawyer and sleazy back-room politico, thunders against the Sodom and Gomorrah of homosexuality at a banquet for the American Society for the Protection of the Family, while across town and light years away, the notorious underground filmmaker of FLAMING CREATURES fame, Jack Smith, in flamboyant harem drag, constructs his own private resistance theater from fragments of Arabian Nights kitsch, avant-garde film feuds, and passionate B-movie camp. Vawter performs both men exquisitely in this film about the closet, where silence is powerful, but from which both of these infamous homosexuals from the repressive and punishing 1950s convey privileged knowledge of Queerness in brilliant performances of their own – Cohn using politics as a form of drag and Smith turning drag into an extraordinary form of politics, pathos, and jouissance. Cohn and Smith had nothing in common except their homosexuality and their death from AIDS in the late 1980s; Vawter, who accepts and produces both men through his own voice and body, would himself die of AIDS, just six months after the film was shot.

Sunday, September 6

4:00 PM
THE LITTLE DEATHS / LAS MUERTES CHIQUITAS
by Mireia Sallarès
In Spanish with English subtitles, 2009, 300 min, digital
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: WHAT GODMILOW TAUGHT

Film Notes

“In 2006 the Barcelona artist and filmmaker Mireia Sallarès began interviewing, in complete intimacy, about thirty Mexican women, about just that: being women in Mexico and their sexual experiences – their experience with pleasure and also with violence. The result is LAS MUERTES CHIQUITAS, ‘the little deaths’, which, like the French ‘la petite mort’, is a slangy euphemism in Spanish for female orgasm, the post-orgasmic state of unconsciousness that some experience after sex. This wild, five-hour film is revolutionary. […] Sallarès uses the simplest of means, filming by herself, entirely in medium close-ups, as she interviews, among many others, two anthropologists, a performance artist, an AIDS worker, a few sex-workers, a cabaret artist, two psychoanalysts, an historian, two ex-nuns, a journalist, a cross-dressing bisexual-tranny, a housekeeper, an actress, a philosopher, two guerillas, even exiled women from other countries…. She asks them to talk about, at first, their own orgasms. What emerge are extraordinary stories and images of pleasure, and often damage.

“The film’s subtitle, ‘An unfinished story of pleasure and violence’, helps connect the dots. There is abundant sexual violence against and around women in Mexico, and effective resistance. Sallarès’s correspondents are prepared to talk about their histories and so the film goes there – not just to the violence but also to the relationship between violence and sexuality, and soon enough to violence, sex, pleasure and spiritual release. These are models to learn from and admire. The critic Helena Braunštajn says this film is a place ‘where pleasure is related to armed struggle, feminicide, transsexuality, women’s liberation theology, prostitution, illness, exile, the plurality of Mexican identity, and the ethical commitment of art to socio-political reality.’ One woman says orgasm is ‘like grabbing onto the wings of an angel who lowers me down to the ground.’ Enough said.” –Jill Godmilow

5:15 PM
EC: ZVENIGORA
by Alexandr Dovzhenko
With Russian intertitles; English synopsis available, 1928, 96 min, 35mm, silent
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

Film Notes

Dovzhenko’s second film, attacked by Soviet critics for being so beautifully rendered as to actually lessen its political impact, remains today a “cinematic poem” as the director named it. Episodic, folkloric, and allegorical, it is a mythic search for hidden treasure by two brothers. Dovzhenko wrote: “I did not so much make the picture as sing it out like a songbird.”

7:30 PM
EC: ARSENAL
by Alexandr Dovzhenko
With Russian intertitles; English synopsis available, 1928-29, 87 min, 35mm, silent
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

Film Notes

“An epic canvas covering Ukrainian history from WWI to the Russian Civil War, as experienced in Kiev, and culminating in fighting around the arsenal in the heart of the city. Dovzhenko essentially uses a static camera, but with much use of montage and cross-cutting. […] Where Dovzhenko is clearly distinctive, however, is his placing of human events against the majestic backdrop of nature, in particular the sky. Man and nature are one, as a dying Bolshevik asks his comrades to transport and bury him in his native soil.” –David C. Gillespie, EARLY SOVIET CINEMA: INNOVATION, IDEOLOGY AND PROPAGANDA

Tuesday, September 8

7:00 PM
TRUE NORTH
by Michèle Stephenson
In English and French with English subtitles, 2025, 96 min, DCP
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

Film Notes

“This propulsive cinematic confrontation with Canada’s anti-Black racism explores the pivotal, yet often overlooked, Canadian civil rights movement. Filmmaker Michèle Stephenson (AMERICAN PROMISE; STATELESS; GOING TO MARS: THE NIKKI GIOVANNI PROJECT) artfully weaves a haunting soundscape with dynamic archival footage and intimate new interviews, immersing us in Black life in 1960s Montreal. The film culminates in the 1969 Sir George Williams Affair, where 200 students, many of them Haitian immigrants fleeing the Duvalier regime, occupied a ninth-floor computer lab at Sir George Williams University (now Concordia) to protest blatant institutional bigotry. This rare footage feels hauntingly prescient against the backdrop of recent student protests, serving as a stark reminder that these cycles of resistance are deeply etched in our collective history. By shining a light on these unsung stories, Stephenson reframes the 1960s civil rights movement not as a strictly American phenomenon, but as a continent-wide, ongoing struggle for survival, justice, and dignity.” –FULL FRAME DOCUMENTARY FILM FESTIVAL

Preceded by:
Dawn Wilkinson DANDELIONS 1995, 5 min, 16mm
“In DANDELIONS, Dawn Wilkinson – a Black Canadian woman – bears witness to the experience of being made to feel like an outsider in one’s own home, in one’s own landscape. At one point, Wilkinson observes, ‘I’m Canadian…It’s popular enough to sell beer, but no one can define what it means. And yet they do, they define it every time they ask me where I’m from.’ DANDELIONS is a beautiful and eloquent film that deploys the techniques of a lyrical, interiorized cinema to lay bare the ways in which Western societies foster an idea of whiteness as ‘neutral’ and everything else as ‘other,’ and to illustrate the psychic toll on those who exist outside this construct.” –Jed Rapfogel, CINEASTE

Total running time: ca. 105 min.

Michèle Stephenson will be here in person!

Wednesday, September 9

6:45 PM
TEACH OUR CHILDREN + INSIDE WOMEN INSIDE
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: CHRISTINE CHOY

Film Notes

Christine Choy & Susan Robeson
TEACH OUR CHILDREN
1972, 35 min, 16mm-to-DCP
This film focuses on the historic 1971 Attica prison rebellion in upstate New York. It targets the conditions that caused prisoners to take drastic steps toward securing their basic rights. The film questions the reactions of prison warden Oswald, New York governor Nelson Rockefeller, and President Nixon, as well as the death of 31 inmates and prison guards from bullets fired by the National Guard. Through on-site footage taken during and following the rebellion, and follow-up interviews with inmates, TEACH OUR CHILDREN relates a powerful message concerning prisoner’s rights and represents an important historical document.

Christine Choy & Cynthia Maurizio
INSIDE WOMEN INSIDE
1978, 21 min, 16mm-to-DCP
This film exposes the daily humiliation regularly faced by women in U.S. prisons using firsthand accounts of inmates at the North Carolina Correctional Center for Women and the Correctional Institute for Women at Riker’s Island, New York. Provocative interviews with these women reveal the anger and frustrations of life behind bars. In spite of the realities of their oppression, their optimism and strength are insurmountable.

Total running time: ca. 60 min.

The screening on Wed, Sept 9 will be introduced by JT Takagi (Third World Newsreel) and will be followed by a reception.

8:30 PM
FROM SPIKES TO SPINDLES + FEI TIEN, GODDESS IN FLIGHT
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: CHRISTINE CHOY

Film Notes

Christine Choy
FROM SPIKES TO SPINDLES
1976, 46 min, 16mm-to-DCP
This raw, gutsy portrait of New York’s Chinatown captures the early days of an emerging consciousness in the community. We see a Chinatown rarely depicted, a vibrant community whose young and old join forces to protest police brutality and hostile real estate developers. With bold strokes, it paints an overview of the community and its history, from the early laborers driving spikes into the transcontinental railroad to the garment workers of today.

Christine Choy
FEI TIEN, GODDESS IN FLIGHT
1983, 26 min, 16mm-to-DCP
Based on the play, “Pigeons”, by Ginny Lim, this film focuses on the meeting between an older immigrant and a younger American-born woman living in NYC’s Chinatown. The linkages in their pasts and possible futures unfold as their friendship grows.

Total running time: ca. 75 min.

The screening on Wed, Sept 9 will be introduced by Mei Lum (W.O.W. Project). The screening on Sun, Sept 13 will be followed by a talk with Professor Minju Bae, NYU.

EC: THE PARSON’S WIDOW
by Carl Th. Dreyer
With Danish intertitles; English synopsis available, 1921, 78 min, 35mm, silent
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

Film Notes

(PRÄSTÄNKAN)

In this lyrical, early Dreyer comedy, a young parson wins a plum parish in 17th-century Norway, but is obliged to marry the widow of his deceased predecessor and pretend his attractive young fiancée is his sister. Dreyer’s touch is evident in the close-ups of the pastor’s would-be rivals and parishioners, and in a slow pan presaging the 360-degree views of VAMPYR.

6:45 PM
TO LOVE, HONOR, AND OBEY
by Christine Choy & Marlene Dann
1980, 55 min, 16mm-to-DCP
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: CHRISTINE CHOY

Film Notes

Shot in battered women’s shelters, urban and suburban neighborhoods, counseling centers, and even in a county jail where a woman has been incarcerated for the murder of her abusive husband, TO LOVE, HONOR, AND OBEY explores the social, psychological, and cultural factors that contribute to violence against women regardless of ethnicity or economic background. Survivors, safe house administrators, counselors, police officers, and male abusers in counseling explore the many factors that contribute to the pervasiveness of this tragic aspect of American family life. A Third World Newsreel production.

The screening will be introduced by Sanjna Selva (A-Doc).

NAMIBIA, INDEPENDENCE NOW + REORIENTING AFRICA
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: CHRISTINE CHOY

Film Notes

Pearl Bowser & Christine Choy
NAMIBIA, INDEPENDENCE NOW
1985, 55 min, 16mm-to-DCP
This moving film was shot inside refugee settlements in Zambia and Angola in the mid-1980s. It examines how exiled Namibians worked to free their country from illegal South African exploitation and prepare for their country's independence. It shows many aspects of their daily life in exile, especially the women, who were at the forefront of the independence struggle. It focuses on the activities of exiled Namibian independence leader General Toivo ya Toivo, filmed just weeks after his negotiated release from a South African prison.

Christine Choy
REORIENTING AFRICA
2016, 37 min, DCP
This later work by Christine Choy focuses on Chinese workers and Chinese economic development in Ghana, Africa.

Total running time: ca. 95 min.

The screening on Thurs, Sept 10 will be introduced by Sanjna Selva (A-Doc).

Film Notes

Shot by the great German cinematographers Karl Freund and Rudolph Maté, MICHAEL concerns the unconsummated homosexual love between a painter and his manipulative, larcenous model. Friday, September 11

6:45 PM
WHO KILLED VINCENT CHIN?
by Christine Choy & Renée Tajima
In English and Taishanese with English subtitles, 1987, 82 min, 16mm-to-DCP
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: CHRISTINE CHOY

Film Notes

Restored by the Academy Film Archive and The Film Foundation, in association with the Museum of Chinese in America. Restoration funding provided by the Hobson/Lucas Family Foundation, with additional support provided by Todd Phillips.

“On a hot summer night in Detroit, Ronald Ebens, an autoworker, killed a young Chinese-American engineer with a baseball bat. Although he confessed, he never spent a day in jail. This gripping Academy Award-nominated film relentlessly probes the implications of the murder in the streets of Detroit, for the families of those involved, and for the American justice system. Not so much a documentary murder investigation as a meticulously constructed meditation on the race relations, economic forces, and failings of the American legal system that comprised the backdrop for the murder of a Chinese-American automotive engineer in Detroit in 1982, WHO KILLED VINCENT CHIN? remains a stirring, absorbing elegy for justice unserved. Drawing from interviews with Chin’s family and friends and Chin’s killer, automotive assembly-line worker Ron Ebens, along with a wealth of archival footage, WHO KILLED VINCENT CHIN? paints a complex and tragically relevant portrait of an America roiled by socioeconomic unease, the crisis of the automotive industry, and the prevalence of xenophobia.” –NEW YORK FILM FESTIVAL

“The most important political documentary of the 1980s.” –Bill Nichols

The screening on Fri, Sept 11 will be introduced by Shannon Lee of Asian American Arts Alliance (A4). The screening on Sun, Sept 13 will be introduced by Gerry Leonard (A-Doc).

7:30 PM
EC: THE PASSION OF JOAN OF ARC
by Carl Th. Dreyer
With Danish intertitles; English synopsis available, 1927-28, 98 min, 35mm, silent
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

Film Notes

(LA PASSION DE JEANNE D’ARC)

Spiritual rapture and institutional hypocrisy are brought to stark, vivid life in one of the most transcendent achievements of the silent era. Chronicling the trial of Joan of Arc in the final hours leading up to her execution, Dreyer depicts her torment with startling immediacy, employing an array of techniques – including expressionistic lighting, interconnected sets, and painfully intimate close-ups – to immerse viewers in her subjective experience. Anchoring Dreyer’s audacious formal experimentation is a legendary performance by Renée Falconetti, whose haunted face channels both the agony and the ecstasy of martyrdom.

“With THE PASSION OF JOAN OF ARC, there occurs a most striking change in both the film-maker’s style and his intensity of thematic concentration. A few potent shots in previous movies hardly promise the unique and brilliant imagery which here bursts forth frame after frame. […] The vision of JOAN is inspired or demoniac. Her passion is observed with clinical detail in the sharp-etched, stark compositions, many relentless close-ups. But this is also loving detail, for Joan is the first of Dreyer’s possessed, a lineage which may be traced through the victims of VAMPYR to Anne in DAY OF WRATH and Johannes in ORDET; characters who work out their passions throughout the process of their films with peculiar intensity and directness, so that identification with the director himself is implicit.” –Ken Kelman, FILM CULTURE

This moving film was shot inside refugee settlements in Zambia and Angola in the mid-1980s. It examines how exiled Namibians worked to free their country from illegal South African exploitation and prepare for their country's independence. It shows many aspects of their daily life in exile, especially the women, who were at the forefront of the independence struggle. It focuses on the activities of exiled Namibian independence leader General Toivo ya Toivo, filmed just weeks after his negotiated release from a South African prison.

Film Notes

“HA HA SHANGHAI is an outlier in [Choy’s] oeuvre. Far more personal than most of her other films, this documentary is a family affair that features her mother and son as characters, and her daughter Ku-Ling Siegel behind the lens. Christine herself describes the film as a ‘documentary journal,’ and while HA HA SHANGHAI begins as a personal history, it soon develops into a Kafkaesque farce. In the film, [Choy] returns to Shanghai after 30 years to search for the title of a house built by her mother. She reconnects with friends of her family and a local choir teacher. She storms into government buildings with frenetic energy, demanding to see paperwork. When things seem dire, Christine visits a fortune teller and a palm reader, grasping at straws lost to time. Through anecdotes and recollections, she interrogates the modernization of China as well as the Cultural Revolution, the events of which caused the family home to be lost in the first place. […] Although HA HA SHANGHAI is rooted in Christine’s personal experience, it tells a larger tale of how much China has changed since she left.” –Violet Columbus & Ben Klein

Restored by the Academy Film Archive and The Film Foundation, in association with the Museum of Chinese in America. Restoration funding provided by the Hobson/Lucas Family Foundation, with additional support provided by Todd Phillips.

“On a hot summer night in Detroit, Ronald Ebens, an autoworker, killed a young Chinese-American engineer with a baseball bat. Although he confessed, he never spent a day in jail. This gripping Academy Award-nominated film relentlessly probes the implications of the murder in the streets of Detroit, for the families of those involved, and for the American justice system. Not so much a documentary murder investigation as a meticulously constructed meditation on the race relations, economic forces, and failings of the American legal system that comprised the backdrop for the murder of a Chinese-American automotive engineer in Detroit in 1982, WHO KILLED VINCENT CHIN? remains a stirring, absorbing elegy for justice unserved. Drawing from interviews with Chin’s family and friends and Chin’s killer, automotive assembly-line worker Ron Ebens, along with a wealth of archival footage, WHO KILLED VINCENT CHIN? paints a complex and tragically relevant portrait of an America roiled by socioeconomic unease, the crisis of the automotive industry, and the prevalence of xenophobia.” –NEW YORK FILM FESTIVAL

“HOTEL NEW YORK can be seen as a description of a fight; the fight of an immigrant with her new city and the fight of a filmmaker with her desire to make films within precarious boundaries. In HOTEL NEW YORK Jackie Raynal plays and wins.” –CAHIERS DU CINÉMA

“One day in New York, I took my linen to a small Chinese laundry. Then I forgot it for a few weeks. When I went back, the laundry wasn’t there anymore, the building had been demolished! I was haunted by the thought of my bedsheets gone forever with the laundry. This experience was the starting point for the NEW YORK HOTEL script. I wanted to write and make this film to show how everything is transient over there. Things change all the time and are immediately replaced, much quicker than in Europe. The story stemmed from my own experience and impressions as a foreigner. It’s a comedy-drama.” –Jackie Raynal, LIBÉRATION

GO GO GO SLOW (book release event!)
Share +

Film Notes

This evening features a rare screening of John Smith’s SLOW GLASS (1988-91) – which uses the art of glassmaking as a prism to explore themes of memory and transformation – preceded by Marie Menken’s ode to New York City on speed, GO! GO! GO! (1964). Both films utilize layered imagery, in different ways, to alter our perception of time and space. The event celebrates the publication of “Frozen Features”, a new book of photographs by Jason Fulford. For nearly thirty years, Fulford has built a practice on the conviction that meaning lives less inside any single photograph than in the sequence and the things that happen around it – individual pictures forced to rhyme, echo, or collapse into dissonance against their neighbors, across books, exhibitions, publishing, and performance. “Frozen Features” pushes that instinct one step further, into a visual language of layers randomly composed from images made between 1996 and 2026. The results invite us to find the mystical lodged inside the everyday, felt before it’s understood. Fulford will introduce the films, and books will be available for purchase.

For more info about “Frozen Features”, visit: https://loosejoints.biz/products/frozen-features

WORK IN PROGRESS / EN CONSTRUCCIÓN
by José Luis Guerín
In Spanish & Catalan with English subtitles, 2001, 127 min, 35mm-to-digital
Share +

This screening is part of: RUBBLE ON SCREEN: THE CINEMA OF DEMOLITION AND DESTRUCTION

Film Notes

Documenting the demolition of homes to make way for the M11 highway in East London, John Smith argues that BLIGHT “exploits the ambiguities of its material to produce new meanings and metaphors, fictionalizing reality through framing and editing strategies.” Though the houses are torn down and the residents move away, Smith also consecrates BLIGHT as an archive of visual and oral memory for the residents. Whereas BLIGHT is unambiguous in its representation of antipathy toward the destruction of a community, José Luis Guerín’s EN CONSTRUCCIÓN navigates the nuanced attitudes of people affected by infrastructural changes in a Barcelona neighborhood. In long-takes of (sometimes staged) interactions and crumbling walls, Guerín and his team of Pompeu Fabra University students capture a community being buried under the promise of a better future.

Preceded by:

Film Notes

“In 1964, an enterprising psychologist (Dr. Everett Shostrom) persuaded a 30-year-old waitress and single mother, to take part in filmed psychotherapy sessions, with three of the most influential psychologists of the 20th century. The resulting series, THREE APPROACHES TO PSYCHOTHERAPY (1965), was primary training material in the field for decades. With the immersive double projection of THE GLORIA OF YOUR IMAGINATION, Reeves creates an intricate, superimposed montage of Gloria’s unguarded sessions with numerous film artifacts of her lifetime: newsreels, home movies, commercials, a beauty pageant, Cold War propaganda, and educational films. The result sees viewers absorbing the culture of that era directly through Reeves’s mix of intimate storytelling and sense of curiosity.” –WEXNER CENTER FOR THE ARTS

MEISHI STREET

In Mandarin with English subtitles., 2006, 85 min, digital

This screening is part of: RUBBLE ON SCREEN: THE CINEMA OF DEMOLITION AND DESTRUCTION

Film Notes

At the end of SPLITTING, a 1974 film recording of a building “cut” radical sculptor and architect Gordon Matta-Clark made to an abandoned family home in suburban New Jersey, the audience is told that the work was “demolished for urban ‘renewal’.” SPLITTING thus becomes an afterimage of a site-specific and self-destructive artistic thesis, but one that is nonetheless arresting in its visual expressiveness and solemn beauty. Conversely, in MEISHI STREET, Zhang Jinli fights tooth and nail to save his restaurant from demolition in preparation for the 2008 Beijing Olympics. Given a digital video camera by U-teque Collective member Ou Ning to document his efforts, Zhang turns the lens on himself as he makes and hangs protest banners outside his restaurant and visits neighbors, projecting the voice of his Dazhalan neighborhood into a condemned future.

Rather than engendering solidarity and empathy through the depiction of destruction of social and material Palestinian life in the present tense, Cynthia Madansky’s STILL LIFE chooses instead to take spectators on a tour of the Occupied Territories after the bulldozers have rumbled through and the bombs have fallen. Hanging its power on aftermath, STILL LIFE reaches instead for a set of festering implications and associations triggered via images, musical composition, and spoken questions. Like many of the other films in this series, NO OTHER LAND preserves in the visual archive what will likely be lost. Shot over the course of five years and by a collective of four directors from Palestine and Israel, NO OTHER LAND shocks in its immediacy and palpable danger as an SOS call from Masafer Yatta, a front line of the Palestinian struggle.

4:15 PM
IN VANDA’S ROOM / NO QUARTO DA VANDA
by Pedro Costa
In Portuguese with English subtitles, 2000, 171 min, DCP
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: RUBBLE ON SCREEN: THE CINEMA OF DEMOLITION AND DESTRUCTION

Film Notes

The second in his Fontainhas trilogy, IN VANDA’S ROOM follows heroin addict Vanda Duarte and a group of struggling slum dwellers as they try to make a life amid the demolition of their Lisbon neighborhood. Between Vanda’s raucous coughing fits and the clicks of her butane lighter, Costa’s extreme long takes, filmed in austere digital video, capture the sound of her built environs collapsing around her. Unlike the Barcelona neighborhood in EN CONSTRUCCIÓN, though, Fontainhas was wiped from the map by city officials, irredeemable in the eyes of the state, its inhabitants moved elsewhere. Today, it no longer stands, but remains embalmed in the images of Costa’s film.

IN VANDA’S ROOM probes the limit of what cinema is and is capable of, not only in its content, which is bleak and harrowing to be sure, but in its form. Like many films in this series, it is uninterested in the distinction between fiction and documentary, choosing instead to capture life in its essence by whatever means necessary. André Bazin wrote that photography, and by extension cinema, satisfied the deep need that man had for an image that was not an approximation, but was the object itself, “freed from the conditions of time and space that govern it.” Sometimes, truth must be freed from the conditions of the objectively real: Costa proclaimed that he filmed some scenes multiple times until they “became fluidly represented and detached of any melodramatic tone.” Often, truth requires some coaxing.

DEMOLITION / CHAIQIAN / 拆·迁
by J.P. Sniadecki
In Mandarin and Sichuanese with English subtitles, 2008, 62 min, DCP
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: RUBBLE ON SCREEN: THE CINEMA OF DEMOLITION AND DESTRUCTION

Film Notes

Using a waist-high camera pointed at the ground and a drone that follows above, Nadav Assor’s GROUND EFFECT takes its name from the phenomenon by which drones and helicopters, in the process of mapping the environment, alter the landscape by displacing the ground’s surface. The objective visual recording thus becomes subjective in its effect on the land. Merging the camera footage into one, Assor points out the unique flaws and irreconcilability of objective and subjective ways of perceiving. Likewise, J.P. Sniadecki’s DEMOLITION / CHAIQIAN, produced in association with the Harvard Sensory Ethnography Lab, shakes loose a firm cinematic sense of perception. Shot over the course of three weeks and following a group of migrant demolition workers and city dwellers in Chengdu, China, DEMOLITION / CHAIQIAN imbues heavy demolition equipment with awkwardness and humor and turns cameras on cameras, all while a city is disappearing underfoot amidst a sonic tank of grinding metal, bursting concrete, and electronic beeps. Conversely, in Viktoria Schmid’s W O W (KODAK), structures reappear as demolished portions of the Rochester Kodak factory emerge from towering dust clouds, rhyming with the Lumière brothers’ DEMOLITION D’UN MUR made over a century prior.

Preceded by:
Viktoria Schmid W O W (KODAK) 2018, 2 min, 35mm-to-DCP
Nadav Assor GROUND EFFECT 2016, 14 min, digital

7:00 PM
STILL LIFE / 三峡好人
by Jia Zhangke
In Mandarin, Jin, and Sichuanese with English subtitles, 2006, 111 min, DCP
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: RUBBLE ON SCREEN: THE CINEMA OF DEMOLITION AND DESTRUCTION

Film Notes

If Jia Zhangke’s breakout film PLATFORM (2000) was about the destruction of China’s social fabric as it transitioned from Mao to Deng Xiaoping, then Jia’s 2006 Golden Lion winner STILL LIFE focuses on the physical destruction of the built environment as the country ventures through another epochal shift. Like Ou Ning’s MEISHI STREET, STILL LIFE is firmly located during what Western observers routinely note as the era of a “rising China.” A few years after the country’s admittance to the WTO, a couple years before Beijing hosted the 2008 Olympics, and during a time of rising GDP, STILL LIFE asks, in literal terms, whether a rising tide indeed lifts all boats. Shot on location in Fengjie, a town along the Yangtze River in central China, the film centers on two people as they search for their spouses in the city, slowly being demolished to make way for the Three Gorges Dam. Slated to be flooded by the dam’s reservoir, the town is replete with hand painted red lines on the sides of buildings that indicate the imminent water levels, offering a stark warning for those below the line to get out while they can. Like Pedro Costa’s IN VANDA’S ROOM, STILL LIFE is filmed on digital video, lending it not only a documentary aesthetic (emblematic of the Urban Generation of Chinese independent filmmakers at the time), but one of uncanny immediacy. Jia, embracing the xianchang spirit of on-the-ground filmmaking, has argued that the documentarian must allow themself to be “seared” by the immediate present. The traces of the people and buildings of Fengjie, though now relocated and demolished, respectively, become irrevocably imprinted on STILL LIFE and its maker.

RUBBLE ON SCREEN: SHORT FILM PGM
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: RUBBLE ON SCREEN: THE CINEMA OF DEMOLITION AND DESTRUCTION

Film Notes

The final program of the series is comprised of shorts that condense the myriad affects elucidated by the preceding works. Here, the wrecking ball and excavator become central players as humans largely exit the drama, leaving inanimate objects the task of carrying high tragedy and comedy. In Milèna Trivier’s elegiac 12 AUGUST 2002, the filmmaker frames the demolition of a brick gable from below and against the sky, a towering sentinel pummeled, its pieces sold for scrap. Conversely, in Jacob Burckhardt’s playful JawwZZZ, bright orange excavators lose their menace and become bumbling figures as they devour concrete and shift twisted metal, construction crews hosing down the creatures as zookeepers would elephants. Critique remains pointed though in Dominic Angerame’s IN THE COURSE OF HUMAN EVENTS, an anti-city symphony that, instead of celebrating the triumphs of urban technological progress, explores the remnants of de-industrialization in a black and white moonscape bereft of human presence.

Dominic Angerame IN THE COURSE OF HUMAN EVENTS (1997, 23 min, 16mm)

Valentin Noujaïm
OCEANIA

Sixteen-year-old Najib luxuriates in his summer days of gaming until his mother informs him of a neighbor’s passing. Taking the keys to their apartment, he quickly discovers an unexpected world of painful questions.

“OCEANIA is an ode to tenderness. To a new generation that carries on our struggles, that seeks to remember whilst also moving forward. A tribute to love, to the dead and martyrs, and to present history being dismantled and destroyed.” –Valentin Noujaïm

Richard Fung
SEA IN THE BLOOD
2000, 26 min, video
“SEA IN THE BLOOD was to be a meditation on race, sexuality and disease, but after working with the material for three years, it was the emotional story that came through. It’s hard to work with such personal material, but in the end the work takes on a life of its own. ‘Richard’ is a character. Because of the subject matter – disease and death – I wanted to avoid sentimentality. I’d like the audience to think as well as feel.” –Richard Fung

Mohammed Soueid

A documentary on the life and ambitions of a young Lebanese trans woman, Khaled El Kurdi. The video follows her journey from soldier to cabaret dancer, in order to raise funds for her gender-affirming operation. Shot in Beirut, CINEMA FOUAD weaves a complex and multi-layered story of sexuality, identity, and desire, and paints a compelling portrait of its subject.

DEMOLITION / CHAIQIAN / 拆·迁
by J.P. Sniadecki
In Mandarin and Sichuanese with English subtitles, 2008, 62 min, DCP
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: RUBBLE ON SCREEN: THE CINEMA OF DEMOLITION AND DESTRUCTION

Film Notes

Using a waist-high camera pointed at the ground and a drone that follows above, Nadav Assor’s GROUND EFFECT takes its name from the phenomenon by which drones and helicopters, in the process of mapping the environment, alter the landscape by displacing the ground’s surface. The objective visual recording thus becomes subjective in its effect on the land. Merging the camera footage into one, Assor points out the unique flaws and irreconcilability of objective and subjective ways of perceiving. Likewise, J.P. Sniadecki’s DEMOLITION / CHAIQIAN, produced in association with the Harvard Sensory Ethnography Lab, shakes loose a firm cinematic sense of perception. Shot over the course of three weeks and following a group of migrant demolition workers and city dwellers in Chengdu, China, DEMOLITION / CHAIQIAN imbues heavy demolition equipment with awkwardness and humor and turns cameras on cameras, all while a city is disappearing underfoot amidst a sonic tank of grinding metal, bursting concrete, and electronic beeps. Conversely, in Viktoria Schmid’s W O W (KODAK), structures reappear as demolished portions of the Rochester Kodak factory emerge from towering dust clouds, rhyming with the Lumière brothers’ DEMOLITION D’UN MUR made over a century prior.

Preceded by:
Viktoria Schmid W O W (KODAK) 2018, 2 min, 35mm-to-DCP
Nadav Assor GROUND EFFECT 2016, 14 min, digital

Total running time: ca. 85 min.

NO OTHER LAND
by Yuval Abraham, Basel Adra, Hamdan Ballal, and Rachel Szor
In Arabic, English, and Hebrew with English subtitles, 2024, 92 min, DCP
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: RUBBLE ON SCREEN: THE CINEMA OF DEMOLITION AND DESTRUCTION

Film Notes

Rather than engendering solidarity and empathy through the depiction of destruction of social and material Palestinian life in the present tense, Cynthia Madansky’s STILL LIFE chooses instead to take spectators on a tour of the Occupied Territories after the bulldozers have rumbled through and the bombs have fallen. Hanging its power on aftermath, STILL LIFE reaches instead for a set of festering implications and associations triggered via images, musical composition, and spoken questions. Like many of the other films in this series, NO OTHER LAND preserves in the visual archive what will likely be lost. Shot over the course of five years and by a collective of four directors from Palestine and Israel, NO OTHER LAND shocks in its immediacy and palpable danger as an SOS call from Masafer Yatta, a front line of the Palestinian struggle.

Preceded by:
Cynthia Madansky STILL LIFE 2004, 15 min, Super-8mm-to-digital. Sound design by Zeena Parkins.

Valentin Noujaïm
BEFORE SHE FORGETS HELIOPOLIS / AVANT D’OUBLIER HELIOPOLIS
2018, 23 min, digital. In French with English subtitles.
“My family have begun to forget their Egyptian roots and, on asking my grandmother Malo to recount the first part of her life in Cairo, I am confronted by the memories of an exiled Arabic woman, lost in a troubled sea of memories, soon to be erased by the passage of time.” –Valentin Noujaïm

Darryl Daley
YOULOGY / NO GHOSTS
2025, 8 min, digital
“YOULOGY / NO GHOSTS explores cyclical motifs of arrival and departure through the artist’s grandmother’s migration to the United Kingdom and her posthumous return to Jamaica, creating a transcendental frame where memory and time merge. In this speculative space, the film navigates beyond the confines of mortality, reimagining a future where inherited stories resist linearity.” –THIRD HORIZON FILM FESTIVAL

Barbara Hammer
OPTIC NERVE
1985, 16 min, 16mm
“[A] powerful personal reflection on family and aging. Hammer employs filmed footage which, through optical printing and editing, is layered and manipulated to create a compelling meditation on her visit to her grandmother in a nursing home. The sense of sight becomes a constantly evolving process of reseeing images retrieved from the past and fused into the eternal present of the projected image. Hammer has lent a new voice to the long tradition of personal meditation in the avant-garde of the American independent cinema.” –John Hanhardt, WHITNEY MUSEUM OF AMERICAN ART

Razan AlSalah 
YOUR FATHER WAS BORN 100 YEARS OLD, AND SO WAS THE NAKBA
2017, 7 min, digital. In Arabic with English subtitles.
“She looks down at her virtual ghost marked with an X. ‘If I were walking, I would have found it, even if it’s not here anymore.’ Oum Amin, a Palestinian grandmother, returns to her hometown Haifa through Google Maps Streetview – today, the only way she can see Palestine. The film consists of images from Google Street View accompanied by an imaginary voiceover written by the artist, that of her grandmother who was never able to return to her hometown in Palestine. This invented memory, narrated in voiceover, is nevertheless set in a real colonial context. In this pixelated, stroboscopic landscape, archival images narrating British and Israeli colonization appear.” –Cinéma du Réel

Caroline Monnet
IKWÉ
2009, 5 min, digital. In Cree and French with English subtitles.
“IKWÉ is an experimental film that weaves the narrative of one woman’s (IKWÉ) intimate thoughts with the teachings of her grandmother, the Moon, creating a surreal narrative experience that communicates the power of thoughts and personal reflection. Made by Anishinaabe artist Caroline Monnet, the film reflects the intergenerational transmission of Indigenous knowledge.” –WINNIPEG FILM GROUP / NATIONAL BOARD OF CANADA 

Jean-Pierre Bekolo
GRANDMA’S GRAMMAR / LA GRAMMAIRE DE MA GRAND’MERE
1996, 8 min, digital. In French with English subtitles.
“An inherited lesson from Djibril Diop Mambéty’s grandmother is transmitted through Jean-Pierre Bekolo’s chronicle of their conversation. Creating a Pan-African exchange, the Cameroonian Bekolo listens to the Senegalese Mambéty root his cinema in his grandmother’s storytelling – a narrative form of returns and repetitions, of continuation and reinvention.” –Yasmina Price

Shenny De Los Ángeles & Amanda Morell (iiritu)
FLORINDA’S DAUGHTER / HIJA DE FLORINDA
2024, 12 min, digital. In English and Spanish with English subtitles.
“Through a series of black-and-white tableaux, this poetry film follows the journey of Young Naomi in Everglades, Florida. She learns from Florinda, her grandmother, about the ancestral practices of caring for the land and nurturing grief in the face of environmental challenges. As the story unfolds, we grow to understand Florinda’s indigenous teachings of controlled burns and the importance of embracing fire rather than suppressing it. As the prescribed burns ignite from Florinda’s hands, an archival portal is birthed.” –BROOKLYN ACADEMY OF MUSIC

Total running time: ca. 85 min.

STILL LIFE / 三峡好人
by Jia Zhangke
In Mandarin, Jin, and Sichuanese with English subtitles, 2006, 111 min, DCP

This screening is part of: RUBBLE ON SCREEN: THE CINEMA OF DEMOLITION AND DESTRUCTION

Film Notes

If Jia Zhangke’s breakout film PLATFORM (2000) was about the destruction of China’s social fabric as it transitioned from Mao to Deng Xiaoping, then Jia’s 2006 Golden Lion winner STILL LIFE focuses on the physical destruction of the built environment as the country ventures through another epochal shift. Like Ou Ning’s MEISHI STREET, STILL LIFE is firmly located during what Western observers routinely note as the era of a “rising China.” A few years after the country’s admittance to the WTO, a couple years before Beijing hosted the 2008 Olympics, and during a time of rising GDP, STILL LIFE asks, in literal terms, whether a rising tide indeed lifts all boats. Shot on location in Fengjie, a town along the Yangtze River in central China, the film centers on two people as they search for their spouses in the city, slowly being demolished to make way for the Three Gorges Dam. Slated to be flooded by the dam’s reservoir, the town is replete with hand painted red lines on the sides of buildings that indicate the imminent water levels, offering a stark warning for those below the line to get out while they can. Like Pedro Costa’s IN VANDA’S ROOM, STILL LIFE is filmed on digital video, lending it not only a documentary aesthetic (emblematic of the Urban Generation of Chinese independent filmmakers at the time), but one of uncanny immediacy. Jia, embracing the xianchang spirit of on-the-ground filmmaking, has argued that the documentarian must allow themself to be “seared” by the immediate present. The traces of the people and buildings of Fengjie, though now relocated and demolished, respectively, become irrevocably imprinted on STILL LIFE and its maker.

7:00 PM
IN VANDA’S ROOM / NO QUARTO DA VANDA
by Pedro Costa
In Portuguese with English subtitles, 2000, 171 min, DCP
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: RUBBLE ON SCREEN: THE CINEMA OF DEMOLITION AND DESTRUCTION

Film Notes

The second in his Fontainhas trilogy, IN VANDA’S ROOM follows heroin addict Vanda Duarte and a group of struggling slum dwellers as they try to make a life amid the demolition of their Lisbon neighborhood. Between Vanda’s raucous coughing fits and the clicks of her butane lighter, Costa’s extreme long takes, filmed in austere digital video, capture the sound of her built environs collapsing around her. Unlike the Barcelona neighborhood in EN CONSTRUCCIÓN, though, Fontainhas was wiped from the map by city officials, irredeemable in the eyes of the state, its inhabitants moved elsewhere. Today, it no longer stands, but remains embalmed in the images of Costa’s film.

IN VANDA’S ROOM probes the limit of what cinema is and is capable of, not only in its content, which is bleak and harrowing to be sure, but in its form. Like many films in this series, it is uninterested in the distinction between fiction and documentary, choosing instead to capture life in its essence by whatever means necessary. André Bazin wrote that photography, and by extension cinema, satisfied the deep need that man had for an image that was not an approximation, but was the object itself, “freed from the conditions of time and space that govern it.” Sometimes, truth must be freed from the conditions of the objectively real: Costa proclaimed that he filmed some scenes multiple times until they “became fluidly represented and detached of any melodramatic tone.” Often, truth requires some coaxing.

7:30 PM
NARROW ROOMS: JERKER
by Hugh Harrison
1991, 90 min, DCP
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: NARROW ROOMS

Film Notes

In a San Francisco apartment, in 1985, Bert is just about to fall asleep when a stranger named J.R. calls. “You hard?” he asks Bert, and the two begin a hot and heavy phone sex session that soon turns into a nightly routine. Over the span of a year, we watch as Bert (Tom Wagner) and J.R. (Joseph Stachura) explore their fantasies, get each other off, and forge a deeper connection that allows them to open up to each other about their fears and sorrows surrounding the AIDS epidemic, all without ever meeting face to face. Playwright Robert Chesley wryly called his groundbreaking 1986 play JERKER “a pornographic elegy with redeeming social value and a hymn to the queer men of San Francisco,” which perhaps sought to preempt the inevitable criticism and censorship of the play’s unabashedly sex-positive dialogue. Hugh Harrison’s smart, rarely seen 1991 adaptation combines the rich, raunchy text of Chesley’s play with the shot-on-video aesthetics of late 1980s gay adult films, making us feel as if we’re watching an especially well-written Jeff Stryker or Joey Stefano movie. Help us celebrate the 40th anniversary of JERKER’s theatrical premiere with this very special screening.

9:00 PM
SCREAMPLAY
by Rufus Butler Seder
1984, 91 min, 16mm-to-DCP
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

Film Notes

Edgar Allan (Rufus B. Seder) is an aspiring screenwriter who has just come to Hollywood to make it in the movies…only to wind up working as the janitor at a fleabag apartment complex run by the greasy ex-boxer Martin (played by underground film legend George Kuchar). When Edgar begins channeling his frustrations with his kooky neighbors into fodder for his latest screenplay, the vivid murder scenes he writes begin to happen for real. As the bodies begin to pile up and the line between reality and fiction become increasingly blurred, Edgar, who is convinced that the only way to be a real writer is to suffer, is slowly driven mad.

SCREAMPLAY is a marvel of campy charm, gothic horror tropes, and astonishingly inventive set design and special effects. Wearing its low-budget resourcefulness on its sleeve, but also genuinely atmospheric and transporting, the spell it casts is all the more remarkable given that it was filmed almost entirely within the confines of the 3,200-square-foot South End Boston loft where director Rufus Butler Seder and his Boston Black and White Movie Company (comprised of fellow students from the city’s School of the Museum of Fine Arts) had previously made a bevy of similarly inspired 16mm short films. Conjured from some of the earliest and still-most-effective cinematic techniques – matte paintings, scale models, ingeniously adaptable sets, animation, highly expressionistic lighting, and the good old-fashioned magic provided by charismatic performers (above all, Seder himself in the central role, and of course the irreplaceable George Kuchar, who broke his ankle during filming of the final fight scene) – SCREAMPLAY is a deliriously entertaining demonstration of the power of low budget invention, and a singularly charming (Boston) salute to Old Hollywood.

Premiered (alongside BLOOD SIMPLE) at the 1985 New York Independent Film Festival, initially distributed by Troma (click here for details about our upcoming Troma series), but rarely screened in recent decades, SCREAMPLAY has been newly restored in 4K – scanned from Seder’s personal 16mm print – and is now back in circulation, where it’s poised to charm, delight, and frighten a whole new audience.

Preceded by:
Rufus Butler Seder
IN THE CITY: A TRILOGY (LIVE IN FEAR; SUN RUN; PHANTOM SUBWAYS)
1977, 6 min, 16mm-to-DCP

BO HARWOOD RECORD RELEASE EVENT: THE KILLING OF A CHINESE BOOKIE
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

Film Notes

This screening is presented on the occasion of the launch of a new LP devoted to the work of Bo Harwood (1946-2022), the composer whose music appears throughout John Cassavetes’s films and whose songs and compositions were often made with Cassavetes’s participation. The record brings together eleven recordings straight from the master tapes held by Bo during his lifetime, including music from THE KILLING OF A CHINESE BOOKIE, A WOMAN UNDER THE INFLUENCE, OPENING NIGHT, and LOVE STREAMS, as well as “Bach Train” and other compositions. The LP will be available for purchase at the screening (with a discounted price for ticket-holders).

The event is organized by Yana Foqué, who initiated the project, with the support of the estate of Bo Harwood. It is hosted by Anthology Film Archives, with support from Grazer Kunstverein, where the LP will also be presented.

John Cassavetes
THE KILLING OF A CHINESE BOOKIE
1976, 108 min (1978 re-release version), 35mm
Cosmo Vittelli (Ben Gazzara) owns a small Los Angeles strip club, the Crazy Horse West. After paying off a gambling debt to a group of gangsters, he finds himself in their debt once again. What begins as a night of obligation gradually pulls Cosmo into a world of violence, performance, loyalty, and survival. Cassavetes follows Cosmo through the clubs, restaurants, cars, and back rooms of Los Angeles, moving between the artificiality of the stage and the uncertain reality beyond it. With its long takes, abrupt shifts in tone, and performances that move freely between theatricality and intimacy, THE KILLING OF A CHINESE BOOKIE is one of Cassavetes’s most elusive and singular films. A classic, the film is graced by a peerless performance from Ben Gazzara as Cosmo.

Conjured from some of the earliest and still-most-effective cinematic techniques – matte paintings, scale models, ingeniously adaptable sets, animation, highly expressionistic lighting, and the good old-fashioned magic provided by charismatic performers (above all, Seder himself in the central role, and of course the irreplaceable George Kuchar, who broke his ankle during filming of the final fight scene) – SCREAMPLAY is a deliriously entertaining demonstration of the power of low budget invention, and a singularly charming (Boston) salute to Old Hollywood.

7:00 PM
A HEART AS WILLING / LA CORAZONADA
by Diego Soto
Chile, In Spanish with English subtitles, 2025, 78 min, DCP
Share +
Twitter Facebook URL

This screening is part of: LOST & FOUND: CINE(MA)S LATINOAMERICANOS RE-UNIDOS

Film Notes

Nieves runs a modest inn with her son in the Chilean countryside, leading a quiet life shaped by routine and deferred dreams. When a wandering motorcyclist arrives and falls for her, the prospect of a late-blooming romance offers an unexpected glimpse of happiness – yet their relationship seems destined to falter. Everything changes with the arrival of a filmmaker who casts them in her adaptation of Shakespeare’s “The Tempest”, drawing them into the creative process and gradually blurring the boundaries between performance and reality. As fiction begins to reshape their everyday lives, new emotional possibilities emerge in this playful and deeply human meditation on love, aging, cinema, and the mysterious ways stories transform those who inhabit them.
